hash-scope.title: Placement is only the first decision
hash-scope.description: A stable key maps to one owner; measurements reveal whether the chosen placement is actually balanced.
hash-scope.note: Key count alone does not measure work.

hash-modulo.title: A changing divisor remaps many keys
hash-modulo.description: With modulo placement, reducing the server pool changes the computed remainder for keys on healthy servers too.
hash-modulo.note: Many cache misses can hit the backing database at once.

hash-ring.title: Clockwise successor owns the key
hash-ring.description: Keys and node tokens share a fixed hash space; each key belongs to the first node clockwise.
hash-ring.note: The ring wraps after its highest token.

hash-membership.title: A new token takes one interval
hash-membership.description: Joining between predecessor P and successor S transfers only the keys in (P, new node].
hash-membership.note: Copy data and catch up writes before durable ownership cuts over.

hash-vnodes.title: Many tokens represent few machines
hash-vnodes.description: Each physical node owns several separated intervals, smoothing random range imbalance.
hash-vnodes.note: More tokens cost more routing and repair metadata.

hash-replicas.title: Ownership and copies are separate
hash-replicas.description: The primary position selects an owner; replica policy places copies on distinct physical failure domains.
hash-replicas.note: One read-hot key needs caching or read replicas, not more tokens.

hash-operate.title: Move a range with a versioned cutover
hash-operate.description: A safe join copies data, catches up concurrent writes, switches the routing version, and verifies results.
hash-operate.note: Track transfer lag and routing-map mismatches.

id-contract.title: Specify the identifier promise
id-contract.description: Uniqueness, size, sort order, and availability are separate requirements.
id-contract.note: An ID is neither authorization nor an exact clock.

id-options.title: Four allocation strategies
id-options.description: A central sequence, leased ranges, UUIDs, and a time-based layout fit different contracts.
id-options.note: Use the simplest approach that meets the stated requirements.

id-layout.title: Budget a 64-bit identifier
id-layout.description: One reserved bit, 41 time bits, 5 data-center bits, 5 machine bits, and 12 sequence bits.
id-layout.note: The timestamp horizon is about 69.7 years from the custom epoch.

id-generate.title: Reserve one sequence slot per call
id-generate.description: Within one millisecond, the worker increments a thread-safe sequence; once full, it waits for time to advance.
id-generate.note: Never wrap a 12-bit sequence in the same millisecond.

id-clock.title: A backward clock needs a safe stop
id-clock.description: The current timestamp must not move behind the worker’s last issued timestamp under the same identity.
id-clock.note: Across regions, time-based IDs are only approximately ordered.

id-workers.title: Lease each live worker identity
id-workers.description: A registry assigns unique worker fields and fences old holders before reuse.
id-workers.note: Two live holders of one worker ID can collide.

id-operate.title: Verify the invariants end to end
id-operate.description: Monitor generator safety and preserve all 64 bits through storage, APIs, and browsers.
id-operate.note: A no-collision sample is not a proof under failure.
